stimuli.text: A block of mass 3 kg on a 30° incline is connected by a light string over a light, frictionless pulley at the top of the incline to a hanging block of mass 5 kg. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the block and the incline is 0.15. The system is released from rest, and the hanging block descends.
A block of mass 1.6 kg on a horizontal frictionless surface is attached to a spring. Its position is $$x(t) = 0.18\cos(6t)$$, with x in meters and t in seconds.
Students measure the period of a simple pendulum for several string lengths, using small amplitudes.
A solid sphere (I = ⅖MR²) and a solid cylinder (I = ½MR²) of equal mass M and radius R are released from rest at the top of the same ramp of height 1.8 m. Both roll without slipping.

questions.stem: A planet has 3 times Earth's mass and 2 times Earth's radius. What is the gravitational field strength at its surface? (Earth's is 9.8 N/kg.)
An oscillator's position is $$x(t) = 0.02\cos(14t)$$ m. What is its maximum speed?
A system obeys $$\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = -49x$$. What is the period of its motion?

options.why: ω is the square root of the coefficient.

questions.stem: Masses of 5 kg and 1 kg hang on either side of a light, frictionless pulley. What is the tension in the string?

options.why: The heavier mass accelerates down, so T is less than its weight.
The lighter mass accelerates up, so T exceeds its weight.

questions.stem: A block slides down a 35° incline. The coefficient of kinetic friction is 0.2. What is the magnitude of its acceleration?

options.why: Correct. a = g(sin θ − μk cos θ).
The component along the incline is mg sin θ.
Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 300$$ N/m is compressed 0.24 m and launches a 0.8 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A cart moving at 28 m/s accelerates uniformly at 4 m/s² over 25 m. What is its final speed?

options.why: Square roots do not add term by term.

questions.stem: A force $$F(x) = 2x$$ N acts along the x-axis. How much work does it do on an object moving from $$x = 1$$ m to $$x = 2$$ m?

options.why: Integrate; do not just evaluate F.

questions.stem: A 1.3 kg mass oscillates on a spring with $$k = 185$$ N/m. What is the period?
Two springs with constants 20 N/m and 40 N/m are connected in parallel and support a 1 kg mass at rest. How far do they stretch in total?

options.why: Series and parallel rules are reversed.
The force is the weight, mg.

questions.stem: A boat points straight across a river 60 m wide, moving at 3 m/s relative to the water. The current flows at 1 m/s. How far downstream does the boat land?

options.why: Correct. The current does not change the time to cross; it only carries the boat downstream.
That is a time, not a distance.

questions.stem: A 2 kg mass hangs from a light string wrapped around a uniform disk pulley of mass 2 kg that turns on a frictionless axle. What is the acceleration of the mass?

options.why: The pulley's inertia reduces the acceleration.
Correct. a = mg/(m + M/2), using I = ½MR² and a = Rα.

questions.explanation: mg − T = ma and TR = ½MR²(a/R) give a = 6.53 m/s².

questions.stem: A 0.2 kg ball hits a wall at 15 m/s and rebounds at 3 m/s. The contact lasts 0.09 s. What is the average force from the wall?

options.why: The velocity reverses, so the speeds add.
Correct. Δp = m(v_f − v_i) with the direction reversed.

questions.stem: A ball rolls off a horizontal ledge 4 m high at 12 m/s. How far from the base of the ledge does it land?

options.why: Horizontal and vertical motion are independent.
Take the square root for the time.
Correct. Fall time from the height, times the horizontal speed.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 2.2 m swings about a pivot at one end with small amplitude. What is its period?

options.why: d is L/2, the distance to the center of mass.
A rod is a physical pendulum, not a simple one.
Correct. T = 2π√(I/(mgd)) with I = mL²/3 and d = L/2.

questions.stem: A car rounds a flat curve of radius 120 m. The coefficient of static friction is 0.7. What is the maximum speed without skidding?

options.why: Correct. Static friction supplies the centripetal force: μmg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: A motor lifts a 260 kg load 14 m at constant speed in 17 s. What average power does it deliver?

options.why: That is the work; divide by time.

questions.stem: A wheel spinning at 44 rad/s slows uniformly to rest in 20 s. How many revolutions does it make while stopping?

options.why: The average angular speed is ω₀/2.
Correct. Δθ = ½ω₀t, then divide by 2π.
That is in radians; convert to revolutions.

questions.stem: A particle's position is $$x(t) = 4t^3 - 5t^2 - 4t$$, with x in meters and t in seconds. What is its acceleration at $$t = 3$$ s?

options.why: That is the velocity; differentiate again.
The derivative of 2bt is 2b, which also remains.
Bring each exponent down as a factor when differentiating.

questions.explanation: a(t) = 24t - 10, so at t = 3 the value is 62.

questions.stem: A spring with $$k = 480$$ N/m is compressed 0.21 m and launches a 0.5 kg block across a frictionless surface. What is the block's speed after leaving the spring?

options.why: The ½ appears on both sides.

questions.stem: A thin spherical shell rolls without slipping from rest down a ramp of height 0.6 m. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Correct. mgh = ½mv²(1 + β) with I = ⅔MR².
That is only correct for a hoop.

questions.stem: A 5 kg cart moving at 9 m/s collides with and sticks to a 7 kg cart at rest. What is their speed after the collision?

options.why: Correct. Momentum is conserved; kinetic energy is not.
Kinetic energy is not conserved here.
Use m₁v₁ for the initial momentum.

questions.explanation: v_f = 5·9/12 = 3.75 m/s; kinetic energy lost = 118 J.

questions.stem: A 49 kg person stands on a scale in an elevator that is accelerating downward at 3 m/s². What does the scale read?

options.why: The acceleration changes the normal force.
Correct. The scale reads the normal force: N − mg = ma (up positive).
Check the direction of the acceleration.

questions.stem: An object's acceleration is $$a(t) = 6t$$ m/s². At $$t = 0$$ it has velocity 8 m/s and is at $$x = 0$$. What is its velocity at $$t = 4$$ s?

options.why: Correct. Integrate a(t) and add the initial velocity.
The acceleration is not constant, so constant-acceleration equations do not apply.

questions.stem: A block starts from rest and slides 2 m down a 30° incline with coefficient of kinetic friction 0.3. What is its speed at the bottom?

options.why: Friction depends on the normal force, mg cos θ.
Correct. mgh − μmg cos θ·L = ½mv².
Use the vertical drop, L sin θ.

questions.explanation: h = 1 m. v = √(2g(h − μL cos θ)) = 3.07 m/s.

questions.stem: A uniform rod of length 1.9 m is pivoted at one end and released from rest in a horizontal position. What is its angular acceleration just after release?

options.why: Correct. τ = Mg(L/2) and I = ML²/3 give α = 3g/(2L).
Use τ = Iα with I = ML²/3.

questions.stem: A uniform 7 m beam weighing 600 N rests on supports at both ends. A 700 N load sits 3 m from the left end. What force does the right support exert?

options.why: That is the left support's force.
The load is not at the center.
Include the beam's weight at its center.
Correct. Take torques about the left support.

questions.stem: A 1 kg ball on a 0.7 m string moves in a vertical circle. At the bottom of the circle its speed is 8 m/s. What is the tension in the string there?

options.why: Check the direction of gravity relative to the center.
Correct. At the bottom, T − mg = mv²/r.

questions.stem: The potential energy of a particle is $$U(x) = 1x^3 - 12x$$ J. At what positive x is the particle in stable equilibrium?

options.why: Correct. Equilibrium where dU/dx = 0; stable at a minimum.
Set the derivative, not U, to zero.

questions.explanation: dU/dx = 3x² − 12 = 0 gives x = 2 m; d²U/dx² > 0 there, so it is stable.

questions.stem: An object of mass 1.1 kg falls from rest with a drag force $$F = -bv$$, where $$b = 0.06$$ kg/s. What is the time constant of its approach to terminal speed?

options.why: τ has units of seconds: m/b.
Correct. From m dv/dt = mg − bv, τ = m/b.

questions.explanation: v_T = mg/b = 180 m/s and τ = m/b = 18.3 s.

questions.stem: Point masses of 1 kg and 2 kg are at the ends of a massless rod 1 m long. What is the rotational inertia about the rod's center?

options.why: Measure from the center, not an end.
Correct. Sum of mr² with r = L/2.
Each mass is L/2 from the center.

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 3 kg and radius 0.2 m spins at 6 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.5 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.
Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.

questions.stem: A constant torque of 6 N·m acts on a wheel ($$I = 2$$ kg·m²) initially at rest, through 10 revolutions. What is the wheel's final angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Work τΔθ (in radians) equals ½Iω².

questions.stem: A uniform disk of mass 6 kg and radius 0.4 m spins at 4 rad/s on a frictionless axle. A 0.75 kg lump of clay is dropped onto the rim and sticks. What is the new angular speed?

options.why: Correct. Angular momentum is conserved: I_iω_i = I_fω_f.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in a sticking collision.

questions.stem: A 4 kg block on a horizontal table is connected by a string over a light pulley to a hanging 1 kg block. The coefficient of kinetic friction between the table and the block is 0.2. What is the acceleration of the blocks?

options.why: Correct. Net force (m₂g − μm₁g) divided by the total mass.
Include friction on the table block.

questions.stem: A 6 kg ball moving at +9 m/s collides elastically head-on with a 7 kg ball at rest. What is the velocity of the 7 kg ball afterward (positive in the original direction)?

options.why: That would be a sticking collision.
Correct. Elastic: conserve momentum and kinetic energy (relative velocity reverses).

questions.explanation: v₁' = (m₁ − m₂)v/(m₁ + m₂) = -0.692 m/s; v₂' = 2m₁v/(m₁ + m₂) = 8.31 m/s.

questions.stem: A 2 kg object at rest experiences a net force $$F(t) = 2t^2$$ N from $$t = 0$$ to $$t = 4$$ s. What is its final speed?

options.why: Correct. Impulse ∫F dt equals the change in momentum.
Divide by the mass to get speed.

questions.stem: A 1500 kg car heading east at 18 m/s collides with a 500 kg car heading north at 14 m/s, and they lock together. What is their speed just after the collision?

options.why: Weight each velocity by its mass.
Momentum is a vector; add components at right angles.
Correct. Conserve momentum in x and y separately, then combine.

questions.stem: A planet has mass $$8 \times 10^{22}$$ kg and radius $$5 \times 10^{6}$$ m. What is the escape speed from its surface? ($$G = 6.67 \times 10^{-11}$$ N·m²/kg²)

options.why: That is the circular orbit speed; escape needs √2 times more.

questions.stem: A 18 g bullet moving at 220 m/s embeds in a 2.9 kg block hanging from strings. How high does the block rise?

options.why: Find the block's speed after the collision first.
Kinetic energy is not conserved in the collision.
Correct. Momentum for the collision, then energy for the swing.

questions.explanation: V = 1.36 m/s after the collision; h = V²/(2g) = 0.094 m.

questions.title: Block on an incline with a hanging mass

parts.prompt: Draw (describe) a free-body diagram for the 3 kg block, labeling each force.

rubric.criterion: Weight down, normal force perpendicular to the incline, tension up the incline.
Kinetic friction down the incline (opposite the motion).

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the acceleration of the system in terms of the masses, θ, μ and g, then calculate its value.

rubric.criterion: Newton's second law applied to each block (or the system).

parts.prompt: Calculate the tension in the string.
Calculate the speed of the blocks after the hanging block has descended 1 m, and the work done by friction on the incline block during that motion.

rubric.criterion: Work by friction, with a negative sign.

parts.prompt: Sketch (describe) graphs of position, velocity and acceleration versus time for one period, aligned vertically.

rubric.criterion: Position is a cosine starting at +A; velocity is a negative sine starting at 0.
rubric.example: x starts at 0.18 m; v starts at 0 and goes negative.

rubric.criterion: Acceleration starts at its negative maximum and is opposite in sign to position throughout.

parts.prompt: Derive expressions for v(t) and a(t), and determine the maximum speed and maximum acceleration.
Calculate the spring constant and the period.
Calculate the total mechanical energy and describe how kinetic and potential energy vary during one period.

rubric.example: K is maximum at x = 0 and zero at x = ±A; U is the reverse; the sum is constant. Each varies twice per period.

parts.prompt: Describe a procedure the students could use to measure the period accurately, including how to reduce uncertainty.

rubric.example: Time 10 swings with a stopwatch and divide by 10.

rubric.criterion: Keep the amplitude small and repeat trials.
rubric.example: Release from under about 10° and average several trials.

parts.prompt: Identify quantities to graph that would give a straight line, and explain how g can be found from the graph.
Plot (describe) the linearized data and draw a best-fit line. Use it to calculate an experimental value of g.
The students repeat the experiment with a much larger amplitude. Predict how the measured periods would change and explain.

rubric.criterion: Periods increase slightly; the small-angle approximation (sin θ ≈ θ) no longer holds.
rubric.example: The restoring torque is less than proportional to θ at large angles.

parts.prompt: Without calculating, predict which object reaches the bottom first. Justify your prediction using energy.

rubric.example: It has the smaller rotational inertia per MR².

rubric.criterion: Justification: less of its energy goes into rotation, so more is translational kinetic energy.

parts.prompt: Derive an expression for the speed at the bottom of an object with rotational inertia βMR², in terms of g, h and β.

rubric.criterion: Energy conservation including both forms of kinetic energy, with v = Rω.

parts.prompt: Calculate the speed of each object at the bottom.

rubric.example: solid sphere: 5.02 m/s; solid cylinder: 4.85 m/s

parts.prompt: Explain whether your derived expression is consistent with your prediction in part (a), and why neither speed depends on M or R.

rubric.criterion: Smaller β gives larger v, consistent with the prediction.
M and R cancel in the energy equation.
rubric.example: Only the shape factor β matters.
